Chapter 7: Intersectionality — Seeing the Whole Story
It’s easy to think that body shame feels the same for everyone, or that there’s just one path to loving yourself. But let’s be honest—life’s a lot messier than that. Each of us moves through the world carrying a mix of identities—race, gender, ability, sexuality, class. These aren’t just labels. They’re threads, weaving together a story that’s yours alone, but also connected to something much bigger.
Think about someone facing not only fatphobia, but racism and ableism, too. Every day becomes a balancing act—navigating spaces that weren’t made with them in mind, answering questions most people never even get asked. The world’s messages about bodies? They aren’t just about size or shape. They’re about who gets to feel safe, who’s allowed to be seen, who’s even allowed to exist without apology.
Most folks only see one slice of this puzzle and miss the bigger picture. But for people living at these intersections, the weight can double—or even triple. It goes way beyond fitting into jeans or making the team. Sometimes, it’s literally about survival.
There’s this memory—a teenager, the only Black girl in her class, always told to “tame” her hair, to “act normal.” She learns early that her body is a battleground, watched by classmates, teachers, even strangers. The message? If she wants to belong, she has to erase pieces of herself. But as she grows up, she finds others who get it. Together, they start to reclaim what was taken, to celebrate what they once hid.
Intersectionality isn’t just a trendy word. It’s a lens—a way of seeing the world that honors all the layers. It asks us to look beyond our own experience, to really listen to stories that sound different from ours. Because the truth is, none of us are free until all of us are free. Liberation for one is tied to liberation for all.
Radical self-love, then, becomes something bigger than just loving yourself. It’s a collective act. It means standing with others, using whatever privilege you have to open doors, to make space, to make sure every voice is heard. It means asking the tough questions, like—who’s missing from this conversation? Whose voices still aren’t being heard?
The work is ongoing. There’ll be uncomfortable moments—realizing that good intentions aren’t always enough. But there’s also so much joy—learning, growing, building bridges with people who are different from you. Intersectionality isn’t a burden. It’s actually a gift. It reminds us that all our liberation is bound together, and that’s what makes this journey worth it.
